title: North American and European temperate biotas share ancestry from Pliocene circumpolar land

fields.label: Label
fields.value: North American and European temperate biotas share ancestry from Pliocene circumpolar land

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The relationship, with very little identity, between the temperate inhabitants of North America and Europe arises because a common biota inhabited the nearly continuous circumpolar land in warmer Pliocene times and then migrated southward, becoming separated and modified on each continent.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: On this view we can understand the relationship, with very little identity, between the productions of North America and Europe,—a relationship which is most remarkable, considering the distance of the two areas, and their separation by the Atlantic Ocean.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XI, “Geographical Distribution”; section “Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world”. Scope: temperate plants and animals of North America and Europe

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch11-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The proposed history yields distinct fossil and phylogeographic predictions for individual clades. Existing coverage is insufficient to make one explanation account for the entire temperate biota.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Infer divergence times and ancestral ranges for temperate sister lineages in North America and Europe, and compare them with Pliocene circumpolar fossils and paleogeography. Support requires northern ancestral ranges and separation dates consistent with southward migration and Atlantic isolation.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Divergence-time uncertainty often spans multiple climatic episodes.

Different clades crossed via different routes and times.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.65
data adequacy: 0.66
operationalizability: 0.81
analysis feasibility: 0.63
data existence: 0.89

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Relatedness of the two temperate biotas, northern fossils, and rough divergence times are all in public compilations. The specific Pliocene timing and a single circumpolar source are softer, because date errors are wide and more than one northern route fits the same trees. The analysis can support or weaken the outline for many clades and not pin down the historical detail.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate divergence times and ancestral areas for temperate clades shared by North America and Europe, and check Pliocene fossils from Arctic landmasses. Divergences much older than the Pliocene, or no northern fossil connection, would count against this history.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Very little identity has no sharp similarity threshold.

A Beringian route and a North Atlantic route both fit a circumpolar source.

Clock dates for the same clade often span more than the Pliocene.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.55
